sections.html:
The southwest corner of Utah belongs to Washington County, which touches Arizona on the south and Nevada on the west. St. George has been the seat since 1856. The county is 2,430 square miles and among the fastest-growing in Utah: 90,354 people in 2000, 138,115 in 2010 and 180,279 in 2020, with a 2025 estimate of 213,670. About 73.0% of households own their home.

Iron County is to the north and Kane County to the east. Utah's lowest elevation, 2,178 feet at Beaver Dam Wash, is in this county. The territorial legislature created Washington County on March 3, 1852, and its boundaries have stood since March 10, 1892.

With 95,342 residents in 2020, St. George is the biggest city outside the Wasatch Front. Santa Clara and Ivins lie west of it, Washington to the east, and Hurricane and La Verkin farther out. Smaller places cluster near Zion and across the north and west. Inside St. George there are more than 20 neighborhoods, including Bloomington, Little Valley, Southgate, Sunbrook, The Ledges, Desert Color and Stone Cliff, so name yours whenever someone is valuing the property. Big irrigated farms in eastern St. George and Washington have given way to housing and commercial lots.

Heat comes first on any Washington County inspection list, then water. In St. George the average July afternoon reaches 101.9 degrees, around 60 afternoons a year top 100, and the rain gauge collects only about 8.8 inches. Monsoon storms arrive between early July and mid-September, and a January 2005 flood on the Santa Clara River destroyed 28 homes.

Elevation changes the story. Pine Valley often collects more than 20 inches of precipitation a year. Expect buyers to ask about an aging cooling system and about any lot near a wash or river.

sections.h2: Which county offices handle property tax
sections.html:
Billing and collection belong to the treasurer, while valuation appeals go through the auditor. Both offices are at 111 East Tabernacle Street in St. George, UT 84770.

OfficeHandlesPhone
TreasurerTax notices, payments, delinquent taxes(435) 301-7720
AuditorBoard of Equalization, Tax Commission appeal forms(435) 301-7220
County AdministrationGeneral county contact(435) 301-7000

Every year real property tax comes due on November 30, whether or not a notice reached you. The county mails each owner a notice and sends payment details to the mortgage company, yet checking the notice for mistakes is your job. When neighbors received one and you did not, ask the treasurer for a copy.

You can send the treasurer a partial payment of $10 or more per parcel whenever you like. The money is applied to interest first, penalty second and tax last. With more than one delinquent year, Utah law makes you pay the newest year first.

Do not count on a payment plan, because the treasurer does not offer them for delinquent taxes. In May the clerk-auditor sells properties that have been delinquent at least five years, announcing the sale in a newspaper roughly four weeks earlier. Tax liens and tax lien certificates cannot be sold under Utah law. Relief programs, among them a circuit breaker program and indigent and hardship abatements, go through the clerk-auditor.

  • Pay the newest year first when several are open.
  • Send at least $10 per parcel if you can only make a partial payment.
  • Call the treasurer before the May sale if a parcel is close to five years behind.

sections.h2: How to appeal your property value
sections.html:
A request for review goes to the Board of Equalization. Utah sets the filing deadline at the later of September 15 or 45 days after the county auditor's notice, and the board then has 60 days from your application to rule.

The application needs your own estimate of fair market value, plus whatever shows that your assessment is out of step with comparable homes. Open the auditor's appeal page when summer starts, because that is where the county posts the close of each year's window. Mid-September is too late to find out you missed it.

Disagree with the board? File Form TC-194 with the county auditor within 30 days of the Notice of Determination, and the auditor forwards it to the Utah State Tax Commission.

Washington County tax is a lien on the parcel, so the bill stays with the house when ownership changes. If the sale closes mid-year, the title company prorates the year's tax, and the settlement statement lists each side's share.

  • Search your parcel in the county's tax notice lookup at outpost.washco.utah.gov.
  • Check whether your lender's escrow account already paid this year.
  • Have the treasurer confirm any back balance before the closing date. Delinquent taxes get paid newest year first.
  • Give the treasurer a new mailing address so notices do not collect at an empty house.

Inherited houses, vacation homes and rentals in St. George and Hurricane make up most of the calls we take. We buy Washington County houses as-is. When back taxes are involved, the balance is paid from proceeds at closing and you see the figure before deciding, so you never bring cash to the table. A cash sale also skips showings and the wait on a buyer's mortgage, and you choose the closing date. Bring the deed, the latest notice and the parcel number to the first conversation.

Call the treasurer at (435) 301-7720 about the amount owed, an older delinquent year or a notice that never came. Valuation and Board of Equalization questions go to the auditor at (435) 301-7220, and anything else can start at County Administration, (435) 301-7000. All three offices are at 111 East Tabernacle Street in St. George.

Because the board must rule within 60 days of an application, and a Tax Commission appeal must be filed within 30 days of the Notice of Determination, a seller with a sale pending should not leave a value dispute for the last minute. If a closing is near, ask the treasurer for the tax figure and hand it to the title company so the settlement statement matches.

Not sure where your Washington County house stands? It costs nothing to ask. Send us the parcel number and the most recent notice, and tell us whether the house is occupied, vacant, inherited or rented. We will look at the balance, tell you what an as-is purchase would involve, and leave the decision with you.

faqs.q: When are Washington County, Utah property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real property tax is due November 30 every year, even if you did not receive a notice. The treasurer accepts partial payments of $10 or more per parcel at any time. The office is at 111 East Tabernacle Street in St. George.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Washington County property value?
faqs.a: File an application with the county Board of Equalization by the later of September 15 or 45 days after the auditor gives notice. Include your own value estimate and comparable evidence. The auditor's office at (435) 301-7220 can confirm the current year's window.

faqs.q: What if I disagree with the Board of Equalization decision?
faqs.a: Appeal to the Utah State Tax Commission with Form TC-194, filed with the county auditor within 30 days after the Notice of Determination.

faqs.q: Does Washington County sell tax liens?
faqs.a: No. Utah law does not allow tax liens or lien certificates to be sold. Instead, the clerk-auditor holds a sale each May for properties delinquent at least five years.

faqs.q: Who pays the property tax when a Washington County house sells?
faqs.a: The title company prorates the tax at closing, and your settlement statement shows the split. We buy houses as-is in Washington County and can work with whatever tax balance is owed.
